original_value: AbstractWhile many image colorization algorithms have recently shown the capability of producing plausible color versions from gray-scale photographs, they still suffer from limited semantic understanding. To address this shortcoming, we propose to exploit pixelated object semantics to guide image colorization. The rationale is that human beings perceive and distinguish colors based on the semantic categories of objects. Starting from an autoregressive model, we generate image color distributions, from which diverse colored results are sampled. We propose two ways to incorporate object semantics into the colorization model: through a pixelated semantic embedding and a pixelated semantic generator. Specifically, the proposed network includes two branches. One branch learns what the object is, while the other branch learns the object colors. The network jointly optimizes a color embedding loss, a semantic segmentation loss and a color generation loss, in an end-to-end fashion. Experiments on Pascal VOC2012 and COCO-stuff reveal that our network, when trained with semantic segmentation labels, produces more realistic and finer results compared to the colorization state-of-the-art.

result.paraphrase: Abstract: Although recent image colorization methods can generate plausible colorized versions of grayscale photos, they remain limited in semantic understanding. To overcome this, we propose using pixel-level object semantics to guide colorization. The key idea is that people perceive and differentiate colors according to the semantic categories of objects. Building on an autoregressive model, we produce image color distributions and sample diverse colored outputs from them. We introduce two ways to integrate object semantics into the colorization model: a pixelated semantic embedding and a pixelated semantic generator. In particular, the network has two branches: one learns the object identity, and the other learns the object colors. The model is trained end to end by jointly optimizing a color embedding loss, a semantic segmentation loss, and a color generation loss. Experiments on Pascal VOC2012 and COCO-stuff show that, when trained with semantic segmentation labels, our network yields more realistic and finer results than the state of the art in colorization.
